Rabbi Shimshon ben Tzadok: The Tashbetz Katan through the Generations
Этот текст представляет собой исторический и богословский очерк о жизни и наследии рабби Шимшона бен Цадока, выдающегося ученика Махарама из Ротенбурга, жившего в XIII веке. Автор описывает создание его главного труда, «Ташбец Катан», который стал уникальным свидетельством верности, поскольку значительная часть галахических постановлений была записана автором во время семилетнего пребывания в тюрьме вместе со своим учителем. Произведение структурировано как сборник кратких законов и описаний личного поведения наставника, дополненный комментариями Рабейну Переца, что превращает его в фундаментальный кодекс ашкеназских обычаев. В конечном итоге текст подчеркивает роль этого труда как связующего звена в передаче еврейской традиции, оказавшего решающее влияние на такие столпы законодательства, как «Арбаа Турим» и «Шулхан Арух».
The Work and Torah Teaching of Rabbi Shimshon ben Tzadok: The Tashbetz Katan through the Generations
The transitional period between the golden age of the Tosafists and the beginning of the period of codification in Ashkenaz and France is marked by the central figure of Rabbi Meir ben Baruch of Rothenburg, the Maharam. However, the historical memory and halakhic teaching of the Maharam were preserved to a great extent thanks to a handful of loyal disciples who saw the documentation of his practices as a religious and historical mission. The most prominent of these disciples is Rabbi Shimshon ben Tzadok, known by the epithet "the Tashbetz Katan," who lived and worked in the 13th century and died in the year 5072 (1312).[1, 2, 3] Rabbi Shimshon's work is not confined to writing a book of halakha; it constitutes a heroic act of cultural preservation under extreme conditions, since a considerable part of his teaching was recorded within the walls of the prison in which his teacher was held.[1, 4] The book Tashbetz Katan is not merely a collection of rulings, but a living testimony to the Jewish way of life at the close of the period of the Rishonim in Ashkenaz, combining abstract Talmudic discussion with everyday halakhic practice.[4, 5]
The Historical and Biographical Background: A Disciple in the Shadow of Bars
The 13th century in Ashkenaz was a period of harsh political and social upheavals for the Jewish communities. Under the rule of Emperor Rudolf I of the House of Habsburg, the decrees and taxes imposed on the Jews were made more severe, which led to an attempt at mass flight by entire communities toward the Land of Israel.[1] At the head of this movement stood the Maharam of Rothenburg, the greatest of the sages of Ashkenaz at that time, who had founded an important yeshiva in the city of Rothenburg on the Tauber River.[6] In 1286 the Maharam was seized in Lombardy by the imperial authorities, apparently following an informer's denunciation, and was imprisoned in the fortress of Ensisheim in Alsace.[1, 3]
Rabbi Shimshon ben Tzadok, as a principal disciple of the Maharam, chose not to abandon his teacher in his difficult years. He accompanied the Maharam during the seven years of his imprisonment, served him in his daily needs and acted as the connecting link between the imprisoned leader and the Jewish world outside.[1, 4] The relationship between the two was unique; Rabbi Shimshon was not only a disciple who heard lessons, but a "shamash" (attendant) who observed every movement, custom and utterance of his teacher under the restrictive conditions of the prison.[1, 4] These observations later became the basis of the book Tashbetz.
Historical Timeline: The Maharam and the Tashbetz Katan
The Book Tashbetz Katan: Name, Structure and Methodology
The name "Tashbetz" is an acronym of "Teshuvat Shimshon ben Tzadok" (the responsum of Shimshon ben Tzadok).[5] It is very important to distinguish between this book and the book of Rabbi Shimon ben Tzemach Duran, which is also called "Tashbetz" (Teshuvot Shimon ben Tzemach). To prevent confusion between the Ashkenazi work of the 13th century and the North African work of the 15th century, it is customary to call Rabbi Shimshon's book "Tashbetz Katan" (the Little Tashbetz).[3, 5, 8] It is interesting to note that according to testimonies in manuscripts, the name "Tashbetz" was given to the work by the Maharam himself during his lifetime, as a token of appreciation for his disciple.[5]
The Structure and Literary Style
The book consists of 591 sections.[4] Unlike classical books of questions and answers that include long correspondences, the Tashbetz Katan is characterized by extreme brevity and by the style of "rulings and customs."[4, 7] Rabbi Shimshon recorded three kinds of information:
Formal rulings: halakhic responses that the Maharam gave to questions in writing or orally.[4, 7]
Ma'aseh rav: a description of the Maharam's personal conduct in everyday situations, on the assumption that every action of a sage is practical halakha.[4]
The author's notes: explanations by Rabbi Shimshon himself clarifying the background of a ruling or a custom.[4]
This style makes the book a source of the first order for understanding Ashkenazi "piety" (chasidut), not in the modern sense of the word, but in the sense of devotion to ancient customs and extra scrupulousness about the details of commandments as an expression of the fear of Heaven.[9]
The Glosses of Rabbeinu Peretz: The Halakhic Dialogue
Over the years, the glosses of Rabbeinu Peretz ben Eliyahu of Corbeil were added to the original text of Rabbi Shimshon.[3, 4] Rabbeinu Peretz, one of the greatest sages of France and one of the last of the Tosafists, visited Germany and formed a personal connection with the Maharam.[10] His glosses are integrated into the book, usually in parentheses, and begin with the word "u-mihu" ("however").[4, 11]
Rabbeinu Peretz's presence in the book is significant because it represents the synthesis between the halakhic tradition of France and that of Ashkenaz.[10] In many places Rabbeinu Peretz comments on the Maharam's custom, sometimes disagreeing with him and sometimes bringing additional proofs that support him.[10, 12] This collaboration, even though it was carried out after the writing of the original text, made the Tashbetz Katan an accepted code throughout Jewish Europe.[3]
His Halakhic Teaching: An Analysis of Selected Topics
The teaching of Rabbi Shimshon ben Tzadok, as reflected in his book, deals mainly with the fields of Orach Chaim (daily and festival law) and of the forbidden and permitted (issur ve-heter), but it also touches on social and economic questions that were relevant to the life of Jews under gentile rule.
Times of the Day and Prayer: Between Stringency and Practice (Section 1)
The section that opens the book deals with the Maharam's daily routine on the eve of the Sabbath and at times of fasting.[4] From this discussion emerge profound insights into the way Rabbi Shimshon understood the concept of halakhic time. The Maharam used to eat the Friday-night Sabbath meal exactly at the time of sunset, and did not wait for actual nightfall, in order to add from the profane to the holy in the most precise way.[4]
On the subject of fasts, Rabbi Shimshon brings the position of the Maharam, which distinguishes between kinds of fasts:
An ordinary individual or public fast: the Maharam was lenient and held that one may eat at sunset and there is no obligation to wait for the appearance of the stars, since the essence of the fast is the "affliction," which has already been achieved during the day.[4]
A fast over a dream: because of its severity, here the Maharam was stringent and instructed to wait until the actual appearance of the stars.[4]
The eve of Tisha be-Av: here he took extra caution and forbade eating already from the beginning of sunset because of the doubt of "bein ha-shemashot" (twilight).[4]
These distinctions teach of a halakhic approach that balances human needs with the sanctity of the occasion, using Talmudic sources from the tractates Eruvin, Ta'anit and Pesachim.[4]
Jewish Identity in the Gentile Space (Section 591)
Section 591 of the book deals with the charged subject of imitating the customs of the gentiles (chukkot ha-goyim). Rabbi Shimshon records the position of the Maharam, which categorically forbids changing one's dress, even down to the level of a shoelace, if the purpose is to blend in publicly among the gentiles.[4] This ruling is based on the discussion in tractate Sanhedrin concerning "a time of persecution" and the sanctification of God's name.[4]
In the context of idolatry, an interesting practice is brought regarding objects that had been used for worship:
Monetary Relations and Interest with Gentiles
One of the most complex subjects in the period of the Rishonim was the Jewish economy, which was based to a large extent on loans. Rabbi Shimshon devotes extensive space to the laws of interest, bringing the rulings of the Maharam that seek to prevent the circumvention of Torah prohibitions through gentile "straw men."[13]
Thus, for example, he forbids a Jew to lend money to a gentile in order that the gentile lend it to another Jew at interest, since in the end this is interest from Jew to Jew.[13] At the same time, in cases of purchasing debts from gentiles, he brings fine distinctions between interest that has already accrued (which may be received) and future interest (which is forbidden).[13] These rulings attest to the attempt to preserve a moral and halakhic backbone within a pressing economic reality.
Rabbi Shimshon's Influence on the World of Halakha and Custom
The work of Rabbi Shimshon ben Tzadok did not amount only to documentation, but to the shaping of the face of Ashkenazi Jewry for generations. The book Tashbetz Katan became one of the most frequently cited sources in the later books of halakhic ruling.
Influence on the "Tur" and the "Shulchan Arukh"
Rabbi Yaakov ben Asher, author of the Turim, used the Tashbetz Katan as a central source for the customs of Ashkenaz, and through him the rulings of the Maharam reached the Shulchan Arukh of Rabbi Yosef Karo and the glosses of the Rema.[4, 14] His influence is especially prominent in the fields of:
The laws of prayer and the synagogue: the details of the customs of standing, bowing and the order of prayer were drawn to a great extent from Rabbi Shimshon's documentation.[4]
The laws of mourning and burial: the Tashbetz Katan serves as a source for permitting members of the Chevra Kadisha (burial society) to take payment for their trouble, a ruling cited to this day in modern responsa.[14]
The laws of ethics and evil speech: the book stresses the importance of "clean language" and respect for fellow creatures as part of the halakhic obligation, and not only as a measure of piety.[15]
The Standing of the "Tashbetz" through the Generations
Rabbi Chaim Yosef David Azulai (the Chida), in his book "Shem ha-Gedolim," devotes a detailed entry to Rabbi Shimshon ben Tzadok, stressing his absolute loyalty to his teacher and the great precision with which the things were written.[3, 9, 16] The Chida notes that "Tashbetz" is an acronym of his name, and that the book was accepted throughout the Jewish diaspora as a supreme authority on the customs of the Maharam.[3, 5]
Summary and Conclusions: The Bridge between Destruction and Preservation
Rabbi Shimshon ben Tzadok was not merely a "ghostwriter" of the Maharam of Rothenburg; he was an architect of halakhic memory.[1, 4] At a time when the Ashkenazi world of Torah faced the danger of collapse because of persecutions and the imprisonment of its leadership, Rabbi Shimshon wisely turned the prison walls into a study hall.[1] His work demonstrates how an oral tradition becomes a written tradition not out of a desire to innovate, but out of a deep anxiety to preserve what exists.[4]
His Torah teaching, as reflected in the book Tashbetz Katan, is characterized by three fundamental principles:
Fidelity to the source: the attempt to record the deed as it was, without unnecessary pilpul.[4, 7]
Geographical synthesis: the combination with the glosses of Rabbeinu Peretz, which created a bridge between Ashkenaz and France.[10]
Halakha as a way of life: the conception that every moment in the life of the sage, even in prison, is a lesson in Torah.[1]
The book Tashbetz Katan remains to this day one of the most influential books in the shaping of Jewish prayer and custom, and an eternal testimony to the self-sacrifice of a disciple toward his teacher and of a sage toward his Torah.[3, 5] The work of Rabbi Shimshon ben Tzadok ensures that even when the leader is physically imprisoned, his spirit and his Torah remain free and give light to future generations.
